gateway-mediated-federation.title: Gateway-Mediated Agent Federation with Containment Preservation
gateway-mediated-federation.novelty_thesis: Combination novelty (KSR): four-way co-location of (1) bilateral cryptographic handshake, (2) per-peer negotiated capability bundle, (3) runtime intent-and-topic enforcement, (4) agents-never-addressable. Closest in-domain prior art (A2A) explicitly chose agent-addressability — strong objective indicia of non-obviousness. Verdict from independent KSR review: DEFENSIBLE.

phase_2_round_1_answers.a2a_relationship: Complement, not compete. A2A is about message shape; OGP is about who is allowed and what they may invoke. A2A connects agents-to-agents; OGP connects gateways-to-gateways. A2A assumes pre-existing trust; OGP establishes bilateral trust without shared identity infra. Scope decisions consistent with their respective threat models, not picking from same menu of solutions to the same problem.

prior_art_landscape_april_28.no_new_direct_competitors: Specific space of bilateral cross-domain agent gateway federation with human approval, signed intents, scope grants — no new entrants in last 25 days.
adjacent_prior_art_to_distinguish: Matrix protocol — federated messaging; no agent intent routing, no per-peer per-intent scope grants, no behavioral policy layer, no project intent abstraction.
ActivityPub / fediverse — async social posts; no scope grants, no rate limits in spec, no human approval handshake.
DIDComm v2 (DIF) — identity layer for verifiable credentials; no gateway boundaries, no scope grants, no behavioral policy, no AI agent containment.
Cosmos IBC — asset/state transfer with consensus; different threat model entirely.
BGP — routes packets; doesn't carry agent intents or apply behavioral policy. OGP borrows BGP peering model but applies to fundamentally different domain.
OAuth 2.0 / OIDC — requires trusted authorization server; not bilateral; not designed for cross-domain peer-to-peer.
MCP (Anthropic) — inside one trust domain; tools, not agents; not a federation protocol.
A2A (Google) — stateless request/response; assumes pre-existing trust; no scope grants, no human approval, no persistent peering with lifecycle.
specifically_not_prior_art: Anthropic/OpenAI 'computer use' — single-domain UI control, not federation
Federated learning (Google FL, Apple FL) — model training, different domain
AI agent frameworks (CrewAI, LangGraph, AutoGen) — orchestration inside one trust domain
Decentralized AI / Bittensor / Akash — compute markets, not communication
Cosmos blockchain ecosystem broadly — asset transfer with consensus, fundamentally different

phase_2_round_1_answers.a2a_objective_indicia_refined_framing: Containment was OUTSIDE A2A's threat model, not considered-and-rejected. STRONGER for non-obviousness: A2A optimized for a different problem (intra-domain enterprise) than OGP solves (cross-domain personal/small-team). Google has world-class engineers (BeyondCorp, OAuth, OpenID Connect) and demonstrated interest in agent communication via A2A itself; their decision NOT to address cross-domain trust establishment is failure-of-others-to-solve indicia under KSR. Recognition of the distinct problem is itself part of the inventive step.
phase_2_round_1_answers.draft_a2a_paragraph_for_disclosure: Google's Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, announced April 2025 and now bundled into Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0 (April 2026), is the closest publicly-shipped technology in the agent-communication space. A2A specifies Agent Cards for capability discovery and typed message exchange, but explicitly assumes that trust between communicating parties is established by the deployment environment — typically a shared identity provider, tenant CA, or pre-existing organizational trust relationship. A2A does not specify a bilateral handshake, per-peer scope grants, rate limits, or human-approval primitives. The choice not to include cross-domain trust establishment in A2A is consistent with its target deployment context and is not a solution to the cross-domain personal/small-team federation problem. Google's decision not to address this space — despite its considerable expertise in cross-domain trust (BeyondCorp, OAuth, OpenID Connect) and its evident interest in agent communication (A2A itself) — is offered as objective evidence that the present invention's combination of bilateral handshake, per-peer scope grants, behavioral policy enforcement, and lifecycle state machine for AI agent gateways was not an obvious extension of the prior art at the time of invention.
